Problem 40 Solution

Author

Author

Statement

Let \(A, B, C\) be sets.

Prove \(A \setminus (B \setminus C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C)\).

Solution

let \(x \in A \setminus (B \setminus C)\). This means \(x \in A\) and \(x \notin (B \setminus C)\). Because \(x \notin B \setminus C\), we know \(x \in B\) and \(x \notin C\) is false. The negation of “\(x \in B\) and \(x \notin C\)” is “\(x \notin B\) or \(x \in C\)”. We now have \(x \in A\), and (\(x \notin B\) or \(x \in C\)). Using the distributive law for statements (Problem 13), (Recall \(P \wedge (Q \vee R) \iff (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R)\)) we then have \(x \in A\) and \(x \notin B\), or \(x \in A\) and \(x \in C\). This means \(x \in A \setminus B\) or \(x \in A \cap C\), which proves \(x \in (A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C)\). Repeat for all \(x \in A \setminus (B \setminus C)\). we have shown \(A \setminus (B \setminus C) \subseteq (A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C)\).

Now let \(x \in (A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C)\). This means \(x \in A \setminus B\) or \(x \in A \cap C\). Suppose first that \(x \in A \setminus B\). then we know \(x \in A\) and \(x \notin B\). Because \(x \notin B\), we know \(x \in B\) and \(x \notin C\) is false, so \(x \notin B \setminus C\). This shows \(x \in A\) and \(x \notin B \setminus C\), proving \(x \in A \setminus (B \setminus C)\). Suppose instead that \(x \in A \cap C\). Then \(x \in A\) and \(x \in C\). Because \(x \in C\), we know \(x \in B\) and \(x \notin C\) is false. Hence we know \(x \notin B \setminus C\). Because \(x \in A\) and \(x \notin B \setminus C\), we have \(x \in A \setminus (B \setminus C)\). Repeat for all \(x \in (A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C)\). we have shown \((A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C) \subseteq A \setminus (B \setminus C)\). \(\blacksquare\)
